Les versets suivants décrivent comment elle parvient jusqu'à l'homme : Dieu fait couler l'eau (la pluie), fend la terre pour la végétation, puis fait pousser les grains, la vigne, la verdure fourragère (qadb), l'olivier, le palmier, les jardins denses, les fruits et le pâturage (abb). Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le sens général : l'eau est la pluie, le grain est ce dont on se nourrit, les fruits sont ceux dont l'homme se régale, et l'abb est le pâturage des bêtes. Ils divergent sur le qadb : Ibn Abbas et Ibn Zayd y voient la luzerne fraîche, al-Hasan le fourrage, et Ibn Atiyya des herbes comestibles. Sur les jardins ghulban, Ibn Abbas dit qu'ils sont des arbres touffus ou élevés, tandis que Qatada et Ibn Zayd y voient des palmiers nobles. Quant à l'abb, Abu Bakr et Umar s'en sont abstenus, comme le rapportent al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir ; al-Zamakhshari estime qu'il vaut mieux s'attacher à la gratitude que chercher son sens exact. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan et Mujahid comprennent que le regard porte sur la nourriture une fois rejetée, afin de réfléchir à la fin de ce monde, mais l'opinion majoritaire est la première. Ces deux lectures, « anna » avec fatha ou kasra, sont jugées valables par al-Tabari.

Ces versets invitent l'homme à considérer la manière dont Dieu a préparé sa nourriture. Les commentateurs expliquent que l'eau versée abondamment est la pluie, et que la fente de la terre désigne son éclatement sous l'effet des plantes qui en sortent : céréales, raisin, plantes fourragères (qadb), olivier, palmier, jardins touffus, fruits et herbages (abb). Ces biens sont un bien-être pour les hommes et pour leurs bêtes. Les exégètes s'accordent pour y voir un argument en faveur de la résurrection, puisque la terre morte se couvre de verdure, et un motif de reconnaissance envers Dieu. Les avis divergent sur le sens de certains termes. Pour le mot qadb, Ibn 'Abbas et al-Dahhak y voient la luzerne ou la verdure fraîche, al-Hasan le fourrage, Ibn 'Atiyya les légumes et plantes comestibles fraîches, et les gens de La Mecque l'appellent le qatt. Pour les jardins ghulb, certains y voient des arbres touffus, d'autres des arbres hauts, d'autres des palmiers nobles ou des troncs épais. Quant à l'abb, Ibn 'Abbas et la majorité y voient le pâturage, al-Dahhak la paille, d'autres les fruits frais ; Abu Bakr et 'Umar ont hésité à l'expliquer. Hafs, Hamza et al-Kisa'i lisent « anna » avec fatha, en apposition à la nourriture, tandis que la plupart lisent « inna » avec kasra, en reprise ; les deux lectures sont admises. Certains rapportent que l'on peut aussi regarder le trajet des aliments dans le corps, mais la plupart retiennent le regard sur la providence divine.

Ce verset invite l'homme à considérer sa nourriture. Les commentateurs expliquent qu'Allah a fait descendre l'eau en abondance, puis a fendu la terre pour la faire germer : céréales, raisin, fourrage vert, olives, palmiers, jardins denses en arbres, fruits et herbages, en jouissance pour les hommes et pour leur bétail. Tous s'accordent à entendre le fendement de la terre comme la germination des plantes, comme le rapportent al-Tabari, al-Samani, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi et al-Jalalayn, et Ibn Kathir retient aussi cette lecture. Sur la lecture, al-Tabari juge valables les deux variantes, « inna » avec kasra comme énoncé nouveau ou avec fatha comme apposition à la nourriture. Les avis divergent sur quelques mots. Le qadb désigne pour Ibn Abbas, Ibn Zayd et al-Tabari la luzerne verte, pour al-Hasan le fourrage, et pour Ibn Atiyya les légumes tendres. Le ghulb désigne pour Ibn Abbas les arbres élevés, pour Qatada et Ibn Zayd les palmiers nobles, pour Mujahid et al-Razi les arbres serrés, et pour al-Zamakhshari et Ibn Kathir des troncs épais. L'abb est pour Ibn Abbas et la majorité le pâturage et l'herbe des bêtes, pour al-Dahhak le foin ou toute plante, pour al-Kalbi toute végétation hors fruits. Abu Bakr et Umar ont hésité à en donner le sens, selon les récits cités par Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi. Pour Ibn Kathir et Ibn Ashur, ce tableau sert aussi à prouver par la résurrection des plantes celle des corps.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset fait partie de l'énumération des bienfaits que Dieu accorde à l'homme à travers sa nourriture. Il lui est ordonné de considérer comment Dieu a préparé son aliment : Il a fait couler l'eau en abondance, puis a fendu la terre pour y faire pousser des plantes, et y a fait germer le grain. Pour la plupart des exégètes, le mot « habb » désigne toutes les céréales récoltées, comme le blé et l'orge, et tout ce qui sert à la nourriture humaine, comme le rapportent as-Samʿani, al-Baghawi, an-Nasafi et as-Suyuti. Tous s'accordent à dire que la pluie est ce qui est versé et que la fente de la terre se fait par la végétation, bien que az-Zamakhshari évoque aussi le labour par les bœufs. Ibn ʿAchour considère que l'attribution de ces actes à Dieu est une métaphore rationnelle, car Il est celui qui décrète les causes. Ces commentateurs ne divergent pas sur le sens général, mais sur les détails des versets suivants. Ibn Kathir, par exemple, considère que les céréales englobent l'ensemble des grains. Al-Hasan al-Basri y voit le fourrage des bêtes. Jalal ad-Din al-Mahalli et as-Suyuti se contentent de citer le blé et l'orge comme exemples, ce qui ne traduit pas un désaccord. Les commentateurs ont aussi discuté la lecture : les Kufiens lisent « anna » avec la fatha, en apposition à la nourriture, tandis que la majorité lit « inna » avec la kasra, en reprise. Tous estiment que ces deux lectures sont admissibles et ont le même sens.

Les commentateurs expliquent que, après avoir évoqué la création de l'homme et sa destinée, Dieu lui ordonne de considérer sa nourriture, c'est-à-dire les végétaux dont il se nourrit et qui le font vivre. Il doit voir comment Dieu a fait couler l'eau, fendu la terre et fait pousser les céréales, la vigne et la verdure fraîche (al-qadb), puis l'olivier, le palmier, les jardins touffus, les fruits et l'herbe (al-abb). Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi rapportent que le qadb désigne la luzerne ou le fourrage vert qu'on coupe à plusieurs reprises, tandis que Hasan al-Basri le réduit au fourrage pour les bêtes; Ibn 'Atiyya estime qu'il couvre les légumes tendres que l'on consomme. Il y a presque unanimité sur le raisin, et sur les céréales comme blé et orge. Pour les jardins (ghulb), al-Tabari cite Ibn 'Abbas et Qatada qui y voient des arbres serrés et touffus, d'autres des arbres hauts ou de gros troncs, et Qatada et Ibn Zayd des palmiers nobles; al-Zamakhshari y voit une image de la vigueur des arbres. Le mot (abb) a fait débat : la plupart y voient le pâturage et l'herbe que mangent les troupeaux, d'autres le chaume ou les fruits frais, et Abu Bakr et Umar ont hésité à en donner le sens. Hafs, Hamza et al-Kisa'i lisent (anna) avec fatha comme apposition à la nourriture, la plupart avec kasra comme phrase nouvelle, deux lectures que al-Tabari juge également valables.

Ce verset fait partie de l'énumération des bienfaits de Dieu envers l'homme à travers sa nourriture : après la descente de la pluie, Dieu fait pousser les céréales, la vigne, le fourrage vert, l'olivier, le palmier, les jardins denses et les fruits, herbages compris, qui sont une jouissance pour l'homme et pour son bétail. Les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que le zaytoun est l'olivier dont on tire l'huile, que le nakhl désigne les palmiers, et que le hadiqa est un jardin entouré d'un mur, al-Sam'ani rapportant même que ce qui n'est pas clos n'est pas un jardin. Pour le mot « ghulban », Ibn 'Abbas l'explique par « élevés », 'Ikrima et Ibn Zayd par « aux troncs et aux milieux épais », Qatada et Ibn Zayd encore par « de nobles palmiers », tandis que Mujahid et Muqatil y voient des arbres serrés les uns contre les autres ; al-Zamakhshari propose plusieurs lectures possibles, entre le jardin épais et les arbres volumineux. Sur le mot « qadb », al-Tabari, Ibn 'Abbas et al-Dahhak y voient la luzerne ou le fourrage vert, al-Hasan le fourrage, et Ibn 'Atiyya des herbes tendres comestibles. Quant à « abb », la plupart y voient le pâturage et l'herbe que mangent les bêtes, al-Dahhak la paille, et Ibn 'Abbas en une autre version les fruits frais ; Abu Bakr et 'Umar ont hésité à en donner le sens. Le verset présente aussi une divergence de lecture : la plupart lisent « inna » avec kasra, comme une reprise, tandis que les Kufiens lisent « anna » avec fatha, en apposition à la nourriture.

Ce verset invite l'homme à considérer sa nourriture, la manière dont Dieu l'a préparée : l'eau versée du ciel en abondance, la terre fendue par la végétation, d'où sortent les grains, la vigne, les herbes fraîches, l'olivier, le palmier, les jardins aux arbres serrés et les fruits et pâturages, en jouissance pour vous et pour vos bêtes. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le sens général : les hadaʾiq sont des jardins, clos ou non, et le mot ghulban désigne des arbres épais et vigoureux. Al-Tabari rapporte plusieurs lectures : pour Ibn ʿAbbas et Qatada, il s'agit d'arbres hauts ou de palmiers nobles ; pour Mujahid et Muqatil, de frondaisons entremêlées ; pour Ikrima, de troncs robustes. Sur le qadb, Ibn ʿAbbas et Ibn Zayd y voient la luzerne fraîche, al-Hasan le fourrage, et les Mecquois appellent ainsi le qatt. Le terme abb est le plus discuté : Ibn ʿAbbas et la majorité y voient le pâturage consommé par les bêtes, al-Dahhak le foin, Ibn Abi Talha les fruits frais. Abu Bakr et ʿUmar ont refusé de trancher et ont blâmé l'excès de précision en la matière. Ibn Kathir retient la lecture la plus large : le fruit pour les hommes, l'herbe pour le bétail. Les lectures de la particule anna, avec kasra ou fatha, n'entraînent pas de divergence de sens majeure.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset fait partie d'une énumération des bienfaits de Dieu envers l'homme au sujet de sa nourriture. Pour la plupart, al-fakiha désigne les fruits des arbres que les hommes mangent, tandis que l'abb désigne ce que mangent les bêtes, c'est-à-dire le fourrage et les pâturages. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan et Ibn Zayd retiennent cette lecture, al-Dahhak y voit la paille, tandis qu'une autre transmission d'Ibn 'Abbas parle de fruits frais. Certains disent que l'abb désigne les fruits secs conservés pour l'hiver. Quant à la fakiha, al-Hasan la définit comme les fruits agréables au goût. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi et Ibn al-Jawzi concilient ces avis en attribuant les fruits aux hommes et le fourrage aux animaux, ce que confirme la fin du verset : « une jouissance pour vous et pour vos troupeaux ». Abu Bakr et 'Umar, selon des récits rapportés, ont hésité à définir l'abb, et 'Umar a jugé qu'insister sur ce mot relevait de la recherche excessive. Al-Zamakhshari et Ibn 'Ashur expliquent que cette réserve ne veut pas dire interdire la méditation, mais qu'il faut d'abord se consacrer à la reconnaissance envers Dieu. Ibn Kathir juge la transmission authentique et la comprend comme une demande de connaître l'espèce précise de la plante. D'autres commentateurs se contentent de noter que la différence entre les deux mots tient à l'usage humain et à l'usage animal.

Ce verset 80:32 précise que Dieu a fait croître les produits mentionnés auparavant, les fruits et le fourrage, comme une jouissance et un bien dont profitent les hommes et leurs bêtes. Les commentateurs expliquent que la fakiha désigne ce que l'homme mange des fruits des arbres, tandis que l'abb est ce que broutent les bêtes. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi et al-Qurtubi rapportent que ce qui se mange revient aux hommes et ce que mangent les troupeaux revient aux animaux. Al-Hasan et Qatada disent que les fruits sont pour vous et l'herbe pour vos bêtes. Ibn 'Atiyya et Abu Hayyan voient dans le mot matà' un nom verbal exprimant la jouissance de ces biens. Al-Zamakhshari et al-Razi soulignent que ce bienfait sert de preuve à l'unicité divine et à la résurrection. Le désaccord porte surtout sur le sens du mot abb, présenté comme le pâturage, le fourrage, la paille ou les fruits frais, et Abu Bakr et Umar, selon al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir, ont hésité à en donner une définition certaine.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset conclut le rappel des bienfaits accordés en ce monde et annonce le jour de la résurrection : lorsque survient la Sakhkha, le grand cri qui assourdit les oreilles. Ils divergent sur sa nature. Al-Hasan y voit la deuxième trompe, que les créatures écoutent attentivement, tandis qu'Ibn Abbas la considère comme un nom du Jour dernier. Al-Khalil et Ibn Qutayba y voient une clameur qui rend sourd, et al-Zamakhshari et al-Razi estiment que ce qualificatif est métaphorique, car les gens y prêtent l'oreille. Les exégètes s'accordent sur le fait qu'en ce jour chacun fuit ses plus proches, frère, mère, père, épouse et enfants, soit préoccupé par son propre sort, soit craignant qu'ils ne réclament leurs droits. Al-Hasan et Qatada citent à ce sujet des exemples de prophètes. Tous affirment que chacun est accaparé par sa propre affaire, et un hadith de 'Aïcha est rapporté sur ce point. Les visages se divisent alors en deux groupes : des visages resplendissants, joyeux et souriants pour les croyants, et des visages couverts de poussière et d'obscurité pour les infidèles. Sur la signification de la qatara, Ibn Zayd la rattache à ce qui s'élève vers le ciel et la ghabara à ce qui retombe sur la terre, Ibn Abbas y voit l'humiliation et la détresse, et al-Kalbi et Muqatil un assombrissement du visage. En somme, le verset décrit l'effroi du Jour dernier et la séparation des hommes en heureux et malheureux.

Ce verset décrit le Jour de la Résurrection, lorsque survient « al-Sakhkha », le cri ou le second souffle qui assourdit les oreilles. Ce jour-là, l'homme fuit ceux qui lui sont les plus proches : son frère, sa mère, son père, son épouse et ses enfants, car chacun est occupé par son propre sort. Les exégètes donnent plusieurs raisons à cette fuite : la crainte qu'ils ne réclament les droits et les torts qui les lient à lui, le désir de ne pas voir ce qui lui arrive, ou la certitude qu'ils ne peuvent lui être d'aucun secours. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi rapportent surtout l'idée de l'occupation de chacun par son propre sort, tandis qu'al-Zamakhshari et Ibn 'Atiyya insistent sur la crainte des réclamations ou l'impuissance des proches. Quant à « al-Sakhkha », Ibn 'Abbas y voit un nom du Jour dernier, tandis que al-Hasan et Ibn Kathir la comprennent comme le second souffle de la trompe, et que Ibn Juzayy la rattache à la surdité causée par un cri intense. Vient ensuite la division des visages : ceux des croyants sont radieux, joyeux et lumineux, ceux des mécréants sont couverts de poussière et d'obscurité, ce que les commentateurs expliquent diversement comme de la poussière, de l'obscurité ou de l'humiliation. Al-Qurtubi, al-Razi et Ibn 'Ashur insistent sur la portée de ce tableau, qui dépasse la seule description de la peur. Le verset est ainsi lu comme une mise en scène de la solitude de chacun face à son sort.

Le verset décrit le jour où retentira le cri qui assourdit les oreilles : l'homme fuira alors ses plus proches, son frère, sa mère, son père, son épouse et ses enfants, tant il sera absorbé par son propre sort. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le sens général : chacun sera occupé par son propre état et ne prêtera attention à personne d'autre. Sur le mot « al-Sakhkha », al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir le rapprochent d'un nom du Jour de la Résurrection, tandis que Mawardi et Ibn al-Jawzi rapportent qu'il s'agit de la seconde trompette, la plupart insistant sur son caractère assourdissant. Quant à la raison de la fuite, al-Baghawi, al-Razi et al-Qurtubi en donnent plusieurs : la violence de l'effroi, la crainte d'être réclamé pour les torts commis envers eux, ou la certitude qu'ils ne pourront rien apporter. Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn Sa'di développent surtout la dimension de la crainte des réclamations. Certains rapportent, sans que tous s'y fient, des récits sur des prophètes qui fuiraient leurs proches ; Ibn Kathir et al-Alusi rapportent ces avis mais les jugent faibles ou peu fiables. Le hadith relatant la question de Aïcha sur la nudité au jour du jugement est cité par plusieurs auteurs, dont Ibn Kathir qui en discute la chaîne de transmission. Les commentateurs concluent que le verset exprime l'extrême gravité de ce jour.

Ces versets décrivent la scène du Jour dernier, lorsque survient la Sakhkha, c'est-à-dire le cri ou le son assourdissant qui rend sourd. Ce jour-là, l'homme fuit ses proches les plus chers : son frère, sa mère, son père, son épouse et ses enfants, car chacun est absorbé par sa propre affaire. Les commentateurs expliquent cette fuite de diverses façons : l'effroi de ce jour, le refus de voir ce qui frappe l'autre, la crainte de réclamations pour les torts commis, ou la conscience qu'ils ne pourront rien apporter. Al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir expliquent surtout que la Sakhkha est un nom du Jour dernier ou du son de la trompette, tandis qu'al-Zamakhshari et al-Razi y voient une image, les gens prêtant l'oreille à ce cri. Al-Mawardi rapporte deux sens : la seconde trompette, ou un nom du Jour dernier. Ibn Atiyya et Ibn al-Jawzi insistent sur l'ampleur de l'épouvante, et Ibn Kathir rapporte des récits sur la frayeur de ce jour. Certains commentateurs, dont al-Baghawi, citent des exemples de prophètes, comme Ibrahim fuyant son père ou Nuh fuyant son fils, tandis qu'Ibn Kathir et al-Alusi tiennent ces récits pour faibles ou peu sûrs. Les versets suivants opposent ensuite deux groupes : les visages des croyants, lumineux et joyeux, et les visages des mécréants, couverts de poussière et de noirceur. Ceux-là sont les mécréants et les débauchés.

Ce verset annonce que, lorsque survient la Sakhkha, nom de la Résurrection ou son cri de trompe, chacun fuira ses proches les plus chers, son frère, sa mère, son père, son épouse et ses enfants, car chacun aura ce jour-là une affaire qui l'occupera et le détournera des autres. Les commentateurs expliquent diversement cette fuite : al-Hasan, Qatada et Ibn Zayd y voient, selon les récits rapportés, un éloignement par crainte qu'ils ne réclament les droits et les torts qui les lient, tandis que d'autres la rattachent à l'effroi qui ne laisse à personne le loisir de penser à autrui. Al-Tabari retient la préoccupation de chacun pour lui-même, et al-Mawardi en donne trois raisons possibles, dont la crainte des réclamations et le fait de ne pas vouloir voir leurs tourments. Al-Zamakhshari et Ibn Juzayy rattachent ce passage à la gravité extrême du jour, et Ibn Kathir le relie à la parole rapportée des prophètes : « Mon âme, mon âme ». Sur le sens de « shan yughnihi », al-Baghawi et al-Jalalayn le comprennent comme une occupation qui détourne de tout autre souci, tandis qu'Ibn Qutayba le lit comme ce qui écarte l'homme de ses proches. Concernant les visages, la plupart des exégètes s'accordent à y voir deux catégories : des visages resplendissants et joyeux, ceux des croyants selon Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi, et des visages couverts de poussière et de ténèbres, ceux des infidèles. Al-Razi, Ibn Kathir et al-Zamakhshari s'accordent sur la gloire et la honte de ces deux états, tandis qu'al-Mawardi propose deux lectures possibles du rire, celui de la joie intérieure ou celui de moquerie envers les mécréants. Le verset se conclut par la désignation des mécréants et des pervers, qu'al-Mawardi distingue comme ceux qui nient Dieu dans leur croyance et ceux qui transgressent dans leurs actes.

Ce verset décrit les visages des gens le Jour de la Résurrection. Les visages des croyants sont « musfira », c'est-à-dire lumineux et resplendissants. Ibn 'Abbas en donne pour cause les veillées nocturnes, al-Dahhak les traces de l'ablution, et 'Ata' le fait d'avoir été couverts de poussière dans le sentier de Dieu. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et la plupart des exégètes retiennent simplement l'idée de clarté et de lumière, tandis qu'al-Mawardi rapporte qu'il peut aussi signifier la joie. Le verset ajoute que ces visages rient et se réjouissent : al-Tabari explique que ce rire vient de la joie du bienfait divin et que l'allégresse vient de l'espoir d'un surcroît, alors qu'al-Mawardi envisage aussi un rire de moquerie envers les mécréants.

Les commentateurs s'accordent à voir dans ce contraste la description des habitants du Paradis face aux habitants du Feu. Les visages couverts de poussière, « ghabara », sont ceux des mécréants. Selon Ibn Zayd, la « qatara » est ce qui s'élève vers le ciel et la « ghabara » ce qui retombe vers la terre ; pour Ibn 'Abbas, il s'agit de honte et d'humiliation ; pour Mujahid, d'opprobre ; pour 'Ata', de noirceur ; pour al-Kalbi et Muqatil, d'obscurcissement du visage. Ibn 'Atiyya comprend la « ghabara » comme l'abattement et le chagrin, et la « qatara » comme la poussière de la terre.

Al-Biqa'i et Ibn 'Ashur remarquent que la mention des bienheureux avant les réprouvés répond au cadre de la sourate, qui honore un croyant. Al-Razi rattache la clarté des visages à la délivrance des attaches du monde.

Ce verset décrit les visages des élus le Jour de la Résurrection : ils sont resplendissants, illuminés par la félicité, joyeux et rayonnants de bonheur pour la grâce et l'agrément qu'ils ont reçus de Dieu. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et la plupart des exégètes comprennent le « ispar » comme l'éclat, tandis que Ibn Abbas rapporte qu'il provient de la prière nocturne, al-Dahhak de l'ablution, et Ata de la poussière endurée dans le sentier de Dieu. Le rire et la joie sont généralement entendus comme un signe de contentement intérieur. Al-Mawardi évoque une autre lecture : ce rire pourrait aussi être une moquerie envers les incroyants, sans qu'il tranche en faveur de cette hypothèse. Al-Razi, quant à lui, rattache l'éclat au dégagement des attaches du monde et à l'union avec le monde sacré, et lit le rire et la joie comme relevant des facultés théorique et pratique. Tous s'accordent à identifier ces visages à ceux des croyants, qu'ils opposent aux visages couverts de poussière et de ténèbres des mécréants. Plusieurs commentateurs rappellent à ce propos le récit d'Aïcha sur la pudeur au jour du rassemblement, où le verset est présenté comme une réponse à son inquiétude.

Le verset décrit les visages de ceux qui ne croiront pas au Jour de la résurrection : ils sont couverts de poussière, c'est-à-dire de ghabara, une poussière sombre et de la tristesse. Les commentateurs expliquent cette poussière de différentes façons. Al-Tabari rapporte qu'elle provient de la poussière des bêtes que Dieu réduira en terre après le jugement, et qu'elle se répand sur les visages des incroyants. Al-Mawardi propose deux lectures : une poussière imposée comme marque d'infamie, ou l'expression de l'affliction qui assombrit le visage. Ibn 'Atiyya et Ibn Juzayy, eux, la décrivent comme l'abattement et le chagrin qui font pâlir le visage de l'affligé.

Le mot qui suit, qatara, est également interprété de plusieurs façons. Ibn 'Abbas y voit l'humiliation et la détresse, Mujahid l'opprobre, 'Ata' l'obscurité, tandis qu'al-Suddi et Ibn Zayd y voient de la poussière, Ibn Zayd précisant que la qatara est ce qui s'élève vers le ciel, et la ghabara ce qui retombe vers la terre. Al-Kalbi et Muqatil parlent de visage assombri. Al-Zamakhshari souligne que le mélange de poussière et de noirceur est le plus laid des aspects.

Les commentateurs s'accordent pour dire que ces visages s'opposent à ceux des croyants décrits juste avant, et que ceux qui les portent sont les mécréants et les débauchés. Ibn Kathir précise que la mécréance est celle du cœur et la débauche celle des actes. Al-Razi rapporte qu'al-Murji'a et al-Khawarij se sont appuyés sur ce passage dans leur débat sur le grand péché, et répond que le verset ne nie pas une troisième catégorie.

Ce verset décrit les visages qui seront couverts de poussière et de ténèbres le Jour du Jugement : ce sont ceux des mécréants, qui furent impies et débauchés dans leurs actes. La plupart des commentateurs entendent le mot « qatara » comme l'obscurité, le noircissement et l'abattement du visage, selon Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Muqatil, al-Kalbi, Ibn Kathir, al-Jalalayn et Abu al-Su'ud. Mujahid y voit l'humiliation, as-Suddi la poussière, tandis qu'Ibn Zayd distingue la qatara, ce qui monte vers le ciel, de la ghabara, ce qui retombe sur la terre. Al-Mawardi rapporte cinq avis proches les uns des autres, portant sur la honte, la tristesse et la noirceur. Al-Razi décrit une noirceur semblable à la fumée, plus effrayante quand elle se mêle à la poussière, comme on le voit sur les visages des Noirs couverts de poussière. Az-Zamakhshari y voit une image de l'union de la mécréance et de la perversité. Ibn 'Ashur note que la poussière peut être une humiliation et que la fuite décrite est celle, par exemple, du croyant qui s'éloigne de ses proches polythéistes. Le sens général, partagé par tous, oppose ces visages à ceux des croyants, illuminés et joyeux.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset clôt la description du Jour de la Résurrection et du tri des hommes en deux groupes : ceux dont les visages sont couverts de poussière et d'obscurité sont les mécréants et les pervers, c'est-à-dire ceux qui ont réuni le déni de la foi et la transgression des limites divines en commettant des interdits. La plupart s'accordent à dire que la mécréance désigne ici le rejet et la dissimulation de la vérité, et que la perversion désigne la sortie de l'obéissance à Dieu, l'abandon des devoirs et la commission des interdits, comme le rapportent al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Jaza'iri. Ibn Kathir voit dans la mécréance une affaire des cœurs et dans la perversion une affaire des actes, tandis qu'al-Nasafi distingue les droits de Dieu (la mécréance) des droits des serviteurs (la perversion). Al-Mawardi propose deux lectures possibles, selon qu'il s'agit de la religion et des actes, ou des droits de Dieu et des droits des hommes. Abu al-Su'ud et al-Shawkani y voient deux qualités inséparables réunies chez ces gens. Al-Razi tire de ce verset un argument dans le débat des murji'ites et des kharijites sur le grand péché, puis répond que le texte ne mentionne que deux groupes sans exclure un troisième. Ibn 'Ashur souligne que la juxtaposition sans conjonction indique que les deux qualités sont réunies chez eux. Al-Alusi et Ibn Sa'di notent que la poussière et l'obscurité les recouvrent en rétribution du déni et de la perversion, et que le verset oppose ainsi l'image du malheur à celle du bonheur qui précède.
en: This opening verse of Surah Abasa describes the Prophet ﷺ frowning and turning away from a blind man, Ibn Umm Maktum, who came to ask him for instruction while he was speaking with leading men of Quraysh. The commentators agree that the one who frowned and turned away is the Prophet ﷺ and that the blind man is Abd Allah ibn Umm Maktum. The verb 'abasa means to scowl or contract the face, and tawalla means to turn away. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the Prophet ﷺ was eager to win these notables to Islam, and that, irritated by the man's repeated interruptions, he turned away. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari see the third-person address as a mark of honour and gentleness toward the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy explain that mentioning his blindness either excuses him or intensifies the rebuke. Ibn 'Ashur sees the rebuke as gradually introduced so that the Prophet ﷺ would not be startled. Al-Razi records the objections of some scholars to a reproach of this kind and answers that the blame concerned an inclination of the heart toward the notables. Al-Qurtubi judges that the act would have been a breach of courtesy had the blind man known the Prophet was occupied, and that God wished to protect the hearts of the poor believers. Ibn 'Uthaymin stresses that the Prophet acted by personal judgment, hoping for the conversion of the notables. The man's name is given as Abd Allah, though Amr is also mentioned.

The commentators explain that the phrase "because the blind man came to him" gives the reason for the rebuke at the start of the surah: the Prophet frowned and turned away because Ibn Umm Maktum came while he was speaking with leading men of Quraysh whom he hoped would accept Islam. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that the blind man kept asking to be taught the Quran and repeated his request without noticing that the Prophet was occupied, and the Prophet disliked being interrupted. Ibn Kathir and several others present this as an effort at persuasion driven by hope for the conversion of the notables. Al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya note that "an" functions as a causal particle meaning "because". The verb may be linked either to "he frowned" or to "he turned away". Al-Tabari also records a reading with a lengthened initial vowel, understood as a reproachful question, with a pause after "he turned away". Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya observe that the Quran names the man by his blindness, which some take as explaining his excuse, while Ibn Juzayy sees it as a general permission to mention a defect when it serves a purpose. The commentators agree the surah is Meccan and that the blind man is Ibn Umm Maktum, but they differ on the identity of the notables, with Qatada naming Ubayy ibn Khalaf, Mujahid naming Utba and Shayba, and others naming additional figures.

This verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ after the rebuke for turning away from the blind man Ibn Umm Maktum. God asks him what could make him know whether the man might purify himself, or whether he might take heed and the reminder benefit him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy explain that tazakka means being purified of sins through righteous deeds and through what he learns from the Prophet, while tadhakkur means being admonished. Ibn Zayd takes it to mean embracing Islam, Ata' takes it to mean faith, and al-Dahhak takes it to mean memorising what is recited to him. Al-Mawardi lists several meanings, including faith, practice and understanding of the religion.

The commentators agree that the rebuke is directed at the Prophet rather than at the blind man. Al-Alusi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Qasimi note the gentleness of the shift from the third person to the second, which softens the reproach and restores closeness with the Prophet. Ibn Ashur and Ibn Sa'di add that the verse illustrates the principle that a known good is not sacrificed for a merely hoped-for one.

Readers differ on the word fa-tanfa'ahu: the majority reading keeps it in the nominative, following yadhdhakkaru, while Asim reads it in the accusative as an answer to la'alla. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan compare this with the reading fa-attali'a in Surah Ghafir. Commentators differ on what the pronoun in la'allahu refers to: most say the blind man, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi also mention the possibility that it refers to the disbeliever whom the Prophet hoped to convert.

This verse gently rebukes the Prophet ﷺ for turning away from the blind man Ibn Umm Maktum, who came asking to be taught while the Prophet was speaking with leading men of Quraysh in hope of their conversion. According to the commentators, the meaning is that God knows what this man might gain: he might purify himself from sins through what he learns, or he might be reminded and benefit from the Qur'anic admonition, so he should not have been neglected. The majority reading 'fa-tanfa'uhu' in the nominative is taken as coordinated with 'yadhdhakkaru', while Asim reads it in the accusative as an answer to 'la'alla'. Nearly all commentators identify the blind man as Abd Allah ibn Umm Maktum and report this episode as the occasion of revelation; al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others add that the Prophet later honoured him and twice appointed him to lead the prayer in Medina. They differ on the pronoun in 'la'allahu': al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi refer it to the blind man, whereas al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan refer it to the disbeliever the Prophet hoped to convert, Abu Hayyan finding that reading unworthy of the Qur'an. The commentators explain 'tazakki' as purification from sins or ignorance, and Ibn Zayd takes it to mean embracing Islam. Ibn Ashur and al-Biqa'i note that purification is mentioned before remembrance, as clearing precedes filling. Several, including al-Qurtubi and al-Zamakhshari, draw the lesson of honouring poor believers and not favouring the rich. Al-Razi and Ibn Hazm regard the act as leaving what was preferable rather than a sin, while other commentators do not decide the question.

The commentators explain that this verse, from Surat Abasa, rebukes the Prophet ﷺ for turning toward a wealthy man while turning away from a blind man who came to learn. In its plain sense, the one who regards himself as self-sufficient, that is, who dispenses with faith and with what the Prophet ﷺ brings, is the one toward whom the Prophet eagerly turns, and there is no blame on the Prophet if that self-sufficient man does not purify himself. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate reports that name Quraysh notables such as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, 'Utba and Shayba, or al-'Abbas, while Ibn Juzayy and Ibn 'Ashur stress that the word refers to the one who thinks he needs no guidance. Al-Mawardi, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir explain that istaghna may mean being wealthy or being independent of God, whereas al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi take it as wealth, and Abu Hayyan argues that wealth does not fit the context of prophethood. The verb tasaddā means to confront, to attend to and to listen; Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read it with a doubled letter, the others without. The commentators agree on the moral lesson: the poor seeker deserves the same attention as the indifferent rich man, and Sa'di, Ibn 'Uthaymin and al-Qasimi draw from this a rule of priority. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the explicit pronoun intensifies the rebuke, while al-Shinqiti recalls that the Prophet is not accountable for those who refuse. Ibn Juzayy and al-Razi add that his duty was only to convey the message.

The commentators explain that the phrase 'As for him who thinks himself self-sufficient, you give him your attention' is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ in a tone of gentle rebuke. He turned towards a wealthy man who had turned away from guidance, hoping that he would purify himself. All agree that the verse reproaches an excessive eagerness to win the powerful. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the revelation followed an occasion when the blind companion Ibn Umm Maktum interrupted the Prophet's conversation with Quraysh leaders to ask to be taught. They name the rich man variously as 'Utba and Shayba, sons of Rabi'a, Umayya ibn Khalaf, or others; the reports differ. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi regard some of these narrations as odd or mistaken. As for the meaning of 'istaghna', al-Qurtubi and al-Razi take it to mean wealth, while Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Razi himself read it as being independent of guidance. On recitation, Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read 'tassaddā' with a doubled letter, the others with a single one; some link the verb to presenting oneself, others to listening. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi observe that the sura enjoins equal treatment of poor and rich in teaching, and that the Prophet adopted this. Finally, 'and it is not upon you that he does not purify himself' means that the messenger's duty is only to deliver the message.

In this verse God gently reproaches His Prophet ﷺ: he bears no blame if the wealthy man, who considers himself self-sufficient, does not purify himself through faith, since his duty is only to convey the message. Most commentators agree that the man in question was a rich notable whom the Prophet hoped to convert, and that the verse teaches not to neglect a poor seeker of knowledge for the sake of an indifferent rich man. They differ on the meaning of purification: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari take it as cleansing from sins and polytheism, while Ibn Zayd and Mujahid stress conversion to Islam, and al-Hasan adds that the verse concerns only the believer. Al-Razi notes that the particle ma may be negative or interrogative expressing reproach, without changing the sense much. Several names have been proposed for the wealthy man, such as Utba, Shayba, Umayya, al-Walid or al-Abbas, but Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan consider these identifications unreliable, and Ibn Kathir reports that the blind man was Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum, whom the Prophet later honoured. Ibn Ashur sees the sentence as a parenthetical clause that lightens the Prophet's burden, and al-Razi stresses that it was not a true sin. Ibn Sa'di concludes that a certain benefit should not be sacrificed for an uncertain one. Al-Zamakhshari also reports that scholars took this lesson to heart, so much so that the poor were treated as princes in the gathering of al-Thawri.

This verse, read together with what precedes it, teaches that the one who comes to the Prophet ﷺ striving eagerly, fearing God, deserves priority of attention, while the self-sufficient man who relies on his wealth and standing should not be pursued at the expense of the seeker. The commentators identify the seeker as the blind companion Ibn Umm Maktum, and say the surah was revealed because the Prophet ﷺ turned away from him while speaking with leading men of Quraysh, hoping for their conversion. The names of those notables differ: al-Tabari and Mujahid mention Utba and Shayba, sons of Rabi'a, while others name Abu Jahl, al-Walid or Umayya ibn Khalaf. Most read the verb yas'a as hurrying on foot, whereas al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as striving to gain good and knowledge. The fear mentioned is for most the fear of God, while some take it as fear of stumbling, since the man had no guide. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur see the rebuke as a lesson in the Prophet's conduct and as an act of ijtihad rather than a grave fault. The passage concludes that the Qur'an is a reminder for whoever wills, recorded in honoured, exalted and pure scrolls carried by noble and obedient angelic scribes.

This part of the verse describes the blind man who comes hurrying to the Prophet ﷺ out of fear of God, while the Prophet had turned away from him to attend to leading Quraysh figures in the hope of their conversion. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi identify the blind man as Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum and explain the fear (khashya) as fear of God. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Jalalayn also allow that it may mean fear of the unbelievers and their harm, or fear of stumbling for lack of a guide; Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir consider the latter view weak. All agree that the rebuke is directed at the Prophet ﷺ for neglecting the one who came seeking guidance in favour of the one who thought himself self-sufficient. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that he afterwards honoured the man, seating him beside him. The commentators differ on the sense of the verb tala, rendered either as occupying oneself or turning away, the two being close in meaning. Ibn Ashur concludes that the reproach concerns the frowning and the turning away, not the effort of independent judgment itself. The exegetes generally hold that the verse requires giving the poor and the rich equal attention in calling to God.

This tenth verse of Surah Abasa rebukes the Prophet ﷺ for turning away from the blind man Ibn Umm Maktum, who came running to learn and fearing God, in order to attend to the leaders of Quraysh. Commentators agree that talahha means to be distracted, to pay no heed, or to feign unawareness, and that the original form was tatalahha, with one of the two taas dropped. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi relate the occasion of revelation: the Prophet, hoping to win over the notables, did not want to interrupt his conversation with them, and the verses came down. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi add that the Prophet later honoured Ibn Umm Maktum, saying, "Welcome to the one for whom my Lord rebuked me." Al-Mawardi and al-Razi stress that the rebuke concerns his conduct, not a grave sin, a view Ibn Ashur also supports, presenting the episode as an instance of prophetic reasoning that differs from the hidden judgment of God; al-Alusi cites Ibn Hazm to the same effect. Ibn Kathir notes that the name of the blind man is most often given as Abd Allah, though Amr is also mentioned. Ibn Sa'di and Ibn Uthaymin draw the lesson that the poor and the rich must be treated equally in teaching and preaching. Al-Qasimi reports that Aisha said that had the Prophet concealed any part of revelation, he would have concealed this rebuke.

The commentators explain that "Kalla" is a rebuke that turns the Prophet ﷺ away from what he did: he frowned at the blind Ibn Umm Maktum and turned toward some notables of Quraysh. The meaning is: do not do this again. As for "Innaha tadhkira", they differ on what the pronoun refers to. Al-Farra', al-Kalbi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy take it to be the surah or its verses, Muqatil takes it to be the Quran, and al-Tabari takes it as the Quran with tadhkira meaning admonition. Ibn Juzayy adds that "whoever wills, remembers it" means to hold it in memory and act on it.

Most explain "fi suhufin mukarrama" as honoured pages, which al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir identify with the Preserved Tablet, while others take them to be the books of the prophets or the codices of the Muslims. "Marfu'a" means elevated in rank or placed in heaven, and "mutahhara" means purified from defilement, or kept from the hands of the devils according to al-Zamakhshari.

On "bi-aydi safara", Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and most scholars say they are the angels, envoys between God and His messengers, or scribes who copy the books. Qatada says they are the reciters of the Quran, and Wahb ibn Munabbih says they are the Companions of the Prophet. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour the angels, and Ibn Juzayy considers this the strongest view. "Kiramin bararatin" speaks of their nobility and obedience, read as dignity and righteousness.

The commentators also report the occasion of revelation: Ibn Umm Maktum interrupted the Prophet while he was speaking with leading men of Quraysh, and the Prophet turned away from him; afterwards he always showed him honour. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur note weaknesses in some chains of this report.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the rebuke addressed to the Prophet ﷺ for turning away from the blind man Ibn Umm Maktum in order to speak with Qurayshi leaders whose conversion he hoped for. The verse states that this surah, or according to some the whole Quran, is a reminder, and whoever wishes may remember it and be admonished, while the one who turns away need not be pursued.

Most agree that remembering here means retaining the message and acting upon it. Ibn Abbas and al-Kalbi take the pronoun to refer to the Quran, while Muqatil reads it as meaning that if God wills, He inspires the person to remember. Al-Zamakhshari, followed by others, explains that whoever wills keeps it in mind without forgetting, the masculine pronoun being used because the reminder carries the sense of remembrance and admonition.

Opinions differ on the honoured sheets that follow. Al-Tabari and Muqatil identify them with the Preserved Tablet, al-Suddi takes them as honoured in God's sight, while Ibn Kathir and others point to the scriptures of the prophets, citing the surah al-A'la. Ibn 'Ashur suggests the pronoun may also refer to God, and that the verse implies one who does not remember has chosen not to be instructed.

Ibn 'Uthaymin explains that this willing falls within divine decree, without the person being compelled, since he is bound by the law to believe. These commentaries thus offer several readings, and none is imposed as a consensus.

This verse describes the Reminder as written in honoured scrolls, exalted and purified, and the commentators focus mainly on who the "safara" are. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that most scholars take them to be angels who carry the revelation between God and His messengers, and Ibn Atiyya also regards this as the stronger view. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid understand them as scribes who copy the books, and al-Farra' supports this sense of the word. Qatada holds that they are reciters of the Quran, while Wahb ibn Munabbih identifies them as the Companions of the Prophet. Al-Tabari concludes that the angels are the most correct reading, since they recite the scriptures and carry messages between God and His prophets. As for the "sahifa", al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi link them to the Preserved Tablet, al-Nasafi sees them as copies taken from it, and others mention the books of the prophets or the codices of the Muslims. Al-Hasan says they are purified from every impurity and cannot be touched by polytheists, and al-Sa'di adds that the protection of the text lies in God's making the angels its messengers. For "kiram barara", al-Kalbi understands honour in the sight of the Lord, al-Hasan understands their distance from sins, and al-Mawardi mentions a sense of generosity toward others. Several scholars cite the hadith of Aisha about the one who recites the Quran fluently being with the noble and righteous scribes, and Ibn Kathir and Ibn Jizzi see this as an honour for the Quran and its bearers.

This passage of Surah Abasa describes the Qur'an as a reminder, recorded in honoured, exalted and purified pages, in the hands of noble and pious scribes. The commentators agree that the pages are honoured, exalted and pure, but they differ on what these qualities mean. Al-Hasan, Ibn Kathir and others take purity to mean freedom from every defilement, while al-Suddi takes it to mean that the pages are protected from being touched by unbelievers or devils. Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and others understand exaltation as being in the seventh heaven or as a high rank with God, and al-Mawardi also mentions being raised above resemblance and contradiction.

As for the safara, most commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, identify them as angels. They differ on their role. For Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid they are scribes who copy the books from the Preserved Tablet, while others see them as envoys carrying revelation between God and His prophets. Qatada identifies them as the Qur'an reciters, and Wahb ibn Munabbih as the Companions of the Prophet. Al-Tabari concludes that they are the angels who carry revelation. On the phrase kiram barara, most explain it as noble before God and obedient, al-Hasan as free from sin, and others as generous towards others.

Several commentators cite the hadith of 'A'isha about the one who recites the Qur'an fluently being with the noble, pious safara, and Ibn Juzayy draws from it that he will receive a reward like theirs.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the rebuke addressed to the Prophet ﷺ for turning away from a blind man in order to attend to the notables of Quraysh. Most agree that the "safara" (scribes) are angels: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi understand them as scribes copying books from the Preserved Tablet, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir favour the view that they are angels who carry the revelation between God and His messengers. Al-Farra' and al-Qurtubi link the word to mediation and reconciliation between people. Qatada takes them to be Qur'an reciters, and Wahb ibn Munabbih takes them to be the Companions of the Prophet; Ibn al-'Arabi notes that the term is, when used absolutely, reserved for angels. Ibn 'Ashur accepts that it may also mean scribes of revelation among the Companions, or messengers.

The commentators agree that the Book is described as honoured, exalted and pure, carried by these noble angels. They differ on the meaning of "barara": al-Suddi takes them to be obedient, al-Tabari to be truthful and sincere, and al-Hasan to be those who keep themselves far from sin. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of 'A'isha about the one who recites the Qur'an together with the noble and pious scribes. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the verse a praise of the Qur'an and its bearers, and a foretelling of the spread of Islam.

This passage of Surah Abasa describes the honoured pages containing the Reminder as held by noble, dutiful scribes. Most commentators, including Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir, identify these scribes as angels, while al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi note that the word also refers to copyists who transcribe books or envoys who carry revelation between God and His messengers. They are called noble before God according to al-Kalbi, or kind towards believers, whom they pray forgiveness for, in the view of al-Kalbi and Abu al-Su'ud, or restrained from sin according to al-Hasan. The word translated as dutiful refers to those who are pious and obedient, and some understand it as truthful, keeping their word. Qatada holds that the scribes are the Quran reciters, and Wahb ibn Munabbih that they are the Companions of the Prophet, but Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy find the angelic interpretation stronger. Ibn Juzayy cites the hadith that one skilled in the Quran is with these noble, dutiful scribes. Ibn Ashur adds that the pages may be the sheets on which the Quran was written, the books of earlier prophets, or a heavenly reality. The overall meaning is that the Quran is preserved with God and conveyed by pure and trustworthy intermediaries.

The verse means that man, understood by most commentators as the disbeliever, is cursed or destroyed, and that his extreme ingratitude toward his Lord despite the favours he has received is astonishing. Most commentators link the verse to the rebuke of the Prophet ﷺ for neglecting Ibn Umm Maktum in favour of Quraysh notables, and see in it a lesson on the arrogance of a being created from a drop of fluid. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir understand qutila as a curse or punishment, while some take it as a mere wish for ruin. As for ma akfarahu, most read it as an exclamation of wonder, whereas al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Nasafi and others also allow an interrogative sense: what drove him to disbelieve? Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy favour the exclamation, and Abu Hayyan calls it the apparent meaning. On who is meant, Mujahid says any disbeliever, al-Dahhak names Umayya ibn Khalaf, and Muqatil names Utba ibn Abi Lahab, whose death by a lion is reported by Ibn Kathir and others. The following verses describe the stages of creation, death, burial and resurrection, offered as proof against denial of the resurrection. On the word sabil, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Suddi take it as the passage out of the mother's womb, Mujahid and al-Hasan as the path of good and evil, while al-Razi combines both meanings.

This verse asks the disbelieving human what he was created from, in order to humble his arrogance: God made him from a drop of semen, then shaped him in stages, from drop to clinging clot to lump of flesh, until his form was complete. The commentators agree that "man" here means the arrogant unbeliever, that the question serves to stress how lowly his origin is, and that "how disbelieving he is!" expresses astonishment at his denial despite the favours he has received. Their main disagreement concerns the meaning of "the way" (al-sabil). Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most early scholars take it as the passage out of the mother's womb, whereas Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd understand it as the path of good and evil, of guidance and error, which Ibn Kathir prefers, while others link it to the path of sound reflection that leads to faith. As for "then He caused him to die and gave him a grave", it means that God assigned him a burial place as an honour, as al-Farra and al-Tabari note, and "when He wills, He will raise him" refers to resurrection. Most exegetes hold that "No!" rejects the man's claim to have fulfilled what was required of him; Mujahid takes this as a general truth that no one ever fully fulfils, while Ibn Abbas limits it to the unbeliever who refused faith. The commentaries add that the next verse, which calls for reflection on food, leads the reader to consider God's provision.

This verse, from Surah Abasa, reminds the reader that man was created from a drop of fluid, and that God then shaped him in successive stages, from drop to clot to lump of flesh, until his form was complete. On the phrase "then He made the way easy for him," the commentators differ: Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi and Muqatil take it to mean easing his exit from the mother's womb, a view al-Tabari favours and Ibn Kathir considers the more apparent sense, while Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd understand it as the clarification of the path of good and evil and the facilitation of acting upon it, which Ibn Kathir also regards as the stronger reading. Al-Mawardi and al-Razi widen the meaning to include reason, capacity and the revelation of scriptures. On death and burial, the commentators agree that God granted the dead the honour of a grave rather than leaving the body to beasts and birds, and that the raising up refers to resurrection. As for "Nay, he has not done what He commanded him," Mujahid holds that no one ever fully fulfils what is obligatory upon him, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Fawrak apply it to the unbeliever who did not believe, and Ibn Kathir links it to the term set by the divine decree. Several scholars note that the passage prepares the argument from human creation and sustenance for the possibility of resurrection.

The verse traces the stages of human creation and fate, combining a reminder of divine favour with an expression of wonder at human ingratitude. The commentators explain that man was created from a drop of fluid, that God shaped him in successive stages, then made the way easy for him, caused him to die, gave him a grave, and will raise him up whenever He wills. The main disagreement concerns the phrase 'then the way He made easy for him'. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi, 'Ikrima and al-Dahhak take it to mean the passage out of his mother's womb, which al-Tabari prefers and which Ibn Kathir finds plausible, while Mujahid, al-Hasan, Muqatil and 'Ata' take it to mean the path of guidance and error, or good and evil, a view Ibn Kathir also considers most likely. Ibn Juzayy regards the first reading as stronger because it follows on from the preceding stages. The phrase 'He made him a grave' is understood by most as meaning that he was given a burial, an honour that sets him apart from carrion, though some read it as an order to bury him. Commentators agree that 'Nay!' is a rebuke, and that 'he has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him' refers to failing one's obligations. Mujahid applies it to all people, whereas Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Fawrak restrict it to the disbeliever. The call to consider one's food is read by most as a reflection on rain, the growth of grain, grapes, olives, dates and fruit, while some take it as a look at the food's passage through the body. The word 'abb', meaning pasture or fodder, received several explanations, and Abu Bakr and 'Umar were cautious about defining it. The occasion of revelation, linked to Ibn Umm Maktum, is reported by several commentators, who differ on which disbeliever is meant, such as 'Utba ibn Abi Lahab, Umayya ibn Khalaf, or any unbeliever in general.

This verse says that God caused man to die after creating him, shaping him and making his path out of the womb easy, then gave him a grave in which he is hidden, as an honour, rather than leaving him exposed like other animals. The commentators agree on the general sense: God made him a person who has a grave. They differ, however, on the meaning of the verb. Al-Tabari and al-Mawardi explain that the dead person is placed in a grave, citing a verse of al-A'sha, while Yahya ibn Salam, as reported by al-Mawardi, holds that it means God appointed someone to bury him. Al-Farra', Abu 'Ubayda, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir say that the one who buries with his own hand is the qabir, and that God is the one who makes him buried, in the manner of the Arab expression 'I cut the tail of the camel and God cut it off'. Al-Alusi and Abu al-Su'ud regard death itself as a blessing, since it leads to eternal life. The phrase that follows, 'then when He wills, He raises him', is taken by the commentators to mean resurrection at the time God chooses. Al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the disbeliever has not fulfilled what he was commanded. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the Arabs hardly believed in the raising of the dead, except in their imaginations.

This passage of Surah Abasa affirms that God resurrects the dead when He wills, answering those who find resurrection implausible. The commentators explain that "then, when He wills, He will raise him up" means He will bring him back to life after death for judgement and recompense. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take inshar to mean resurrection, while al-Alusi and al-Qasimi stress that the time of resurrection is unknown to people and depends on God's will, unlike death and burial, which follow the usual course of lives. The phrase "nay, he has not fulfilled what He commanded him" is read by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir as the human failure to discharge his duties; Mujahid takes it generally, that no one ever fully fulfils all that is required of him, whereas Yahya ibn Salam restricts it to the unbeliever who did not believe. There is broad agreement that the context targets the arrogant disbeliever who denies resurrection, and that the verses argue from human creation out of a drop of fluid, from his guidance, death and burial, and from the growth of plants that feed him. Ibn Ashur notes that burial is an honour which Islam affirmed in contrast with pre-Islamic practices. There is no notable legal disagreement in this passage; the differences concern the meaning of inshar, of burial, and the scope of the verse.

The commentators explain that the verse "No! He has not yet fulfilled what He commanded him" is a rebuke to the disbelieving human who considers himself free of obligation, meaning that he has not carried out what God commanded in faith and obedience. They differ on its scope. Mujahid holds that it applies to all people, since no one ever fully fulfils everything God has prescribed. Yahya ibn Salam says it refers specifically to the unbeliever who has not believed or obeyed. Ibn Kathir favours the reading that God's decree to raise the dead has not yet been carried out and will not be until the appointed time has run its course. Ibn Abbas understands it as failure to keep the covenant taken from the loins of Adam. Al-Zamakhshari and those who follow him see it as a conclusion to the account of the stages of creation, death and resurrection, from which the human being nonetheless draws no lesson. Ibn Atiyya and most exegetes say that the human is then invited to reflect on his food, that is, on how water and earth produce the crops, so as to infer the resurrection. Ibn Ashur suggests that "kalla" may refute the denial of resurrection, while al-Hasan takes it to mean "indeed". The commentators present these views without choosing between them, agreeing on the purpose: to remind the human of his failings and of God's favours.

This verse calls man to look at his food: how God determined and arranged it so that it becomes the means of his life. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi explain this looking as reflection and contemplation, and the food as what both people and animals eat. The following verses describe how it reaches man: God pours down water, splits the earth for growth, and brings forth grain, grapes, green fodder (qadb), olives, palms, dense gardens, fruit and pasture (abb). The commentators agree on the broad sense: the water is rain, the grain is what is eaten, the fruits are what people enjoy, and the abb is pasture for animals. They differ on the qadb: Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd take it to be fresh clover, al-Hasan takes it as fodder, and Ibn Atiyya as edible herbs. On the dense gardens (ghulban), Ibn Abbas says they are tall or thickly grown trees, while Qatada and Ibn Zayd understand them as noble palms. As for the abb, Abu Bakr and Umar refrained from defining it, as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report; al-Zamakhshari argues that it is better to focus on gratitude than to pursue its exact meaning. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid understood the looking as directed at the food after it has been expelled, to reflect on the end of this world, but the majority take the first meaning. Al-Tabari considers both readings of "anna", with fatha or kasra, to be valid.

These verses call on man to reflect on his food and how God prepared it. The commentators explain that the water poured forth is the rain, and that splitting the earth refers to its cracking open for growth. The plants that emerge, namely grain, grapes, fodder (qadb), olives, palm trees, dense gardens, fruits and pasture (abb), are provision for humans and their livestock. The commentators agree that the verses offer proof of resurrection, since dead earth is revived with greenery, and that they call for gratitude. They differ on several terms. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak take qadb to mean fresh fodder or clover, al-Hasan takes it as fodder, Ibn 'Atiyya as fresh edible herbs and vegetables, and the people of Mecca call fresh fodder qatt. As for the gardens described as ghulb, some understand them as densely intertwined trees, others as tall trees, others as noble palms or thick trunks. On abb, Ibn 'Abbas and most scholars say it is pasture, al-Dahhak says straw, and others say fresh fruit; Abu Bakr and 'Umar hesitated to explain it. On the reading, 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read anna with a fatha as an apposition to food, while the majority read inna with a kasra as a fresh sentence, and both readings are accepted. Some add that the verse may refer to the path of food through the body, but most keep the focus on God's providence.

This verse invites a person to reflect on his food. The commentators explain that God poured down water abundantly and then split the earth to bring forth growth: grain, grapes, green fodder, olives, palm trees, dense gardens, fruits and pasture, as provision for people and their livestock. They agree that the splitting of the earth means the sprouting of plants, as al-Tabari, al-Samani, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and the Jalalayn state, and Ibn Kathir also takes this view. On recitation, al-Tabari considers both readings of "inna", with kasra as a new statement and with fatha as an apposition to the food, to be correct. Opinions differ on some words. Qadb means green alfalfa for Ibn Abbas, Ibn Zayd and al-Tabari, fodder for al-Hasan, and tender vegetables for Ibn Atiyya. Ghulb means tall trees for Ibn Abbas, noble palm trees for Qatada and Ibn Zayd, closely packed trees for Mujahid and al-Razi, and thick trunks for al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir. Abb means pasture and herbage eaten by animals for Ibn Abbas and most scholars, dry straw for al-Dahhak, and any plant other than fruit for al-Kalbi. Abu Bakr and Umar hesitated to define it, according to reports cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur also see in the revival of plants a proof of the resurrection of bodies.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a list of blessings that God grants humans through their food. Man is told to consider how God prepared his sustenance: He poured water abundantly, then split the earth so that plants could grow, and made grain sprout in it. For most exegetes, the word habb refers to all harvested grains, such as wheat and barley, and anything that feeds people, as recorded by as-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi, an-Nasafi and as-Suyuti. They all agree that the rain is what is poured, and that the splitting of the earth happens through vegetation, although az-Zamakhshari also mentions ploughing by oxen. Ibn 'Ashur holds that attributing these acts to God is a rational metaphor, since He ordains the causes. These scholars do not disagree on the general meaning, but on the details of the following verses. Ibn Kathir, for example, takes the grains to include all kinds of grain. al-Hasan al-Basri understood it as fodder for animals. Jalal al-Din al-Mahalli and as-Suyuti simply cite wheat and barley as examples, which does not reflect a disagreement. The scholars also discussed the recitation: the Kufans read anna with a fatha, as an apposition to the food, while the majority read inna with a kasra, as a new sentence. All considered both readings acceptable and equivalent in meaning.

The commentators explain that after mentioning the creation of man and his destiny, God commands him to look at his food, meaning the plants on which he feeds and lives. He should see how God poured down water, split the earth and made grain, grapes and green fodder (al-qadb) grow, then olives, palm trees, dense gardens, fruit and pasture (al-abb). Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand qadb as fresh fodder such as clover, cut repeatedly, while al-Hasan regards it as animal feed; Ibn 'Atiyya takes it to include tender herbs eaten by people. There is near agreement that the grapevine and grains such as wheat and barley are meant. On the dense gardens (ghulb), al-Tabari reports Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada saying they are thickly intertwined trees, others that they are tall or thick-trunked trees, and Qatada and Ibn Zayd that they are noble palms; al-Zamakhshari reads the image as one of strong, thick trees. The word (abb) is debated: most take it as pasture grazed by livestock, others as straw or fresh fruit, and Abu Bakr and Umar both hesitated to define it. Hafs, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (anna) with fatha as an apposition to the food, most read it with kasra as a new sentence, and al-Tabari considers both readings valid.

This verse belongs to the list of God's favours on man through his food: after the rain, God makes grain, grapes, green fodder, olives, palm trees, dense gardens and fruits grow, all as provision for people and their livestock. The commentators agree that the olive (zaytun) is the tree from which oil is pressed, that the palms are date palms, and that a hadiqa is a garden enclosed by a wall, al-Sam'ani adding that an unenclosed plot is not a garden. On the word ghulban, Ibn 'Abbas says tall, 'Ikrima and Ibn Zayd thick-trunked and thick-middled, Qatada and Ibn Zayd noble palms, while Mujahid and Muqatil say densely intertwined trees; al-Zamakhshari allows several readings, either dense gardens or large trees. On qadb, al-Tabari, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak take it as fresh clover or green fodder, al-Hasan as animal feed, and Ibn 'Atiyya as tender edible herbs. For abb, most take it as pasture grazed by animals, al-Dahhak as straw, and Ibn 'Abbas in one report as moist fruit; Abu Bakr and 'Umar hesitated to define it. The verse also has a reading difference: most read inna with a kasra as a new clause, while the Kufans read anna with a fatha, in apposition to the food.

This verse calls on the human being to look at his food and consider how God prepared it: water poured down in abundance, the earth split open to bring forth grain, grapes, fresh fodder, olives, palms, dense gardens and fruits and pasture, as provision for you and your livestock. The commentators agree on the general meaning: hada'iq are walled or enclosed gardens, and ghulban describes trees that are thick, massive and tightly interlaced. Al-Tabari records several explanations: according to Ibn Abbas and Qatada, they are tall trees or noble palms; according to Mujahid and Muqatil, dense foliage intertwined; according to Ikrima, trunks of great girth. On qadb, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Zayd understand fresh clover, al-Hasan understands fodder, and the people of Mecca call qatt by this name. The word abb is the most debated. Ibn Abbas and most scholars take it as pasture grazed by animals, al-Dahhak as straw, and Ibn Abi Talha as fresh fruit. Abu Bakr and Umar hesitated to define it and rejected excessive speculation on the point. Ibn Kathir keeps the broad reading: fruit for people, herb for cattle. The readings of anna, with kasra or fatha, do not significantly change the meaning.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a list of God's favours to man concerning his food. For most of them, fakiha refers to the fruits of trees that people eat, while abb refers to what animals eat, that is, fodder and pasture. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd hold this reading, al-Dahhak takes it to mean chaff, and another report from Ibn 'Abbas says it means fresh fruits. Some say abb means dried fruit stored for winter. As for fakiha, al-Hasan defines it as the fruits that are pleasant to eat. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi reconcile these views by assigning fruit to people and fodder to animals, which the closing phrase "a provision for you and your livestock" supports. According to reports, Abu Bakr and 'Umar hesitated to define abb, and 'Umar considered insisting on the word to be excessive inquiry. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur explain that this restraint does not forbid reflection, but asks that gratitude to God come first. Ibn Kathir judges the chain of this report sound and reads it as a wish to know the exact kind of plant. Other commentators simply note that the difference between the two words lies in human use versus animal use.

Verse 80:32 says that God caused the things listed before it to grow, the fruits and the pasture alike, as a provision and benefit for people and their livestock. The commentators explain that fakiha refers to the fruits of trees that people eat, while abb is what the animals graze on. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report that what humans eat belongs to them and what the herds eat belongs to the animals. Al-Hasan and Qatada say that the fruit is for you and the fodder for your cattle. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan take matā' as a verbal noun expressing enjoyment of these gifts. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that this favour is cited as evidence of God's oneness and of the resurrection. The main disagreement concerns the word abb, understood as pasture, fodder, straw, or fresh fruit, and Abu Bakr and Umar, as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report, were reluctant to define it with certainty.

The commentators explain that this verse concludes the reminder of God's blessings in this world and turns to the Day of Judgment: when the Sakhkha comes, the great cry that deafens the ears. They differ on what it is. Al-Hasan and others say it is the second blast, to which creatures attentively listen, while Ibn Abbas reports that it is a name of the Day of Resurrection. Al-Khalil and Ibn Qutayba describe it as a shout that deafens, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi take the description as metaphorical, since people lend their ears to it. The commentators agree that on that day a person flees from his closest relatives, brother, mother, father, spouse and children, either because he is preoccupied with his own state or fears they will claim their rights from him. Al-Hasan and Qatada cite examples of prophets in this regard. All agree that each person has a matter that occupies him entirely, and a hadith from 'A'isha is reported on this point. Faces then divide into two groups: radiant, joyful and smiling faces for the believers, and faces covered with dust and darkness for the disbelievers. On the meaning of qatara, Ibn Zayd links it to what rises toward the sky and ghabara to what settles on the earth, Ibn Abbas understands it as humiliation and distress, and al-Kalbi and Muqatil as a darkening of the face. In sum, the verse describes the terror of the Last Day and the division of people into the blessed and the wretched.

This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when the Sakhkha arrives, the shriek or second blast that deafens the ears. On that day a person flees from those closest to him: his brother, mother, father, spouse and children, because each is absorbed in his own state. The commentators offer several reasons for this flight. Some, such as al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi, say it is fear of being called to account for the wrongs and debts between them. Others say it is so as not to see what he suffers, or because he knows they cannot help him, a view given by al-Baghawi and al-Razi. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di emphasise the overwhelming terror and the self-preoccupation that leaves no room for others. Scholars differ on the meaning of Sakhkha: Ibn 'Abbas holds that it is one of the names of the Day of Judgment, while al-Hasan, al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi take it as the second blast of the Trumpet, and Ibn Juzayy derives it from deafening. The verse then divides people into two groups. The faces of believers are bright, smiling and joyful, while the faces of disbelievers are covered with dust and darkness, which the exegetes interpret variously as dust, blackness, humiliation or gloom. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite the hadith of 'A'isha about people being gathered barefoot and naked, while al-Alusi calls the reports about the parents of the Prophet unreliable. The verse is therefore read as a vivid image of human solitude before one's destiny.

The verse describes the day when the deafening blast comes, and a person will flee even from his closest kin: his brother, mother, father, spouse and children, so absorbed will each be in his own condition. The commentators agree on this general meaning: each person will be occupied with himself and will pay attention to no one else. On the word al-Sakhkha, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir link it to a name of the Day of Resurrection, while al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that it refers to the second blast of the trumpet, most stressing that it is so loud that it deafens. As for the reason for the flight, al-Baghawi, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi offer several: the intensity of terror, the fear of being held to account for wrongs done to them, or the certainty that they cannot help. Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di emphasise the fear of their demands. Some report accounts of particular prophets fleeing their relatives; Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi mention these but consider them weak or unreliable. Several authors cite the hadith of Aisha asking about nakedness on the Day of Judgement, and Ibn Kathir examines its chain. The commentators conclude that the verse conveys the extreme gravity of that day.

These verses describe the Day of Resurrection, when the Sakhkha comes, a deafening blast or cry that stuns the ears. On that day a person flees from his nearest kin: his brother, mother, father, spouse and children, because each is preoccupied with his own state. The commentators explain the flight in several ways: the terror of that day, not wanting to see what befalls the other, fear of being held to account for wrongs done to them, or knowing they cannot benefit him. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the Sakhkha is a name of the Last Day or of the trumpet blast, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi also note that people listen attentively to it. Al-Mawardi gives two views: the second blast, or a name for the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi emphasise the severity of the terror. Al-Baghawi and others cite examples of prophets fleeing their relatives, such as Ibrahim from his father and Nuh from his son, while Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi regard some of these reports as weak. The verses then contrast two groups: the faces of believers, bright and joyful, and the faces of disbelievers, covered with dust and darkness. Those are the disbelievers and the wicked.

This verse describes what happens when the Sakhkha arrives, a name for the Resurrection or its blast of the trumpet. On that day a person will flee from the closest people to him, his brother, mother, father, spouse and children, because each will have an affair that occupies him and keeps him from thinking of others. Commentators explain this flight in several ways. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, as reported, understand it as withdrawal out of fear of being held to account for the wrongs and rights between them, while others tie it to the terror of that day which leaves no room for concern for anyone else. Al-Tabari emphasises that each is preoccupied with himself, and al-Mawardi offers several reasons, among them fear of their claims and not wanting them to see his state. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy link the verse to the extreme gravity of the day, and Ibn Kathir connects it to the report of the prophets saying 'my soul, my soul'. On the phrase 'shan yughnihi', al-Baghawi and the Jalalayn read it as an occupation that absorbs a person entirely, while Ibn Qutayba reads it as what turns a man away from his kin. The verse then describes two kinds of faces. Most commentators, including Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, identify the bright and joyful faces as those of the believers, and the faces covered with dust and darkness as those of the disbelievers. Al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari agree on the honour of the first state and the shame of the second, while al-Mawardi suggests two readings of the laughter, as inner joy or as mockery of the unbelievers. The verse ends by naming the disbelievers and the wicked, which al-Mawardi distinguishes as those who deny God in belief and those who transgress in deeds.

This verse describes the faces of people on the Day of Resurrection. The faces of the believers are "musfira", meaning bright and radiant. Ibn 'Abbas attributes this to night prayer, al-Dahhak to the traces of ablution, and 'Ata' to having been dusty in God's way. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most commentators retain the general sense of brightness and light, while al-Mawardi reports that it may also mean joy. The verse goes on to say these faces laugh and rejoice. Al-Tabari explains the laughter as joy at the blessings God has given and the rejoicing as hope for more, while al-Mawardi also considers a laughter of mockery at the disbelievers.

The commentators agree that this contrast describes the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire. The faces covered in dust, "ghabara", belong to the disbelievers. Ibn Zayd says "qatara" is what rises toward the sky and "ghabara" what settles toward the earth; Ibn 'Abbas takes it as humiliation and distress, Mujahid as disgrace, 'Ata' as blackness, and al-Kalbi and Muqatil as the darkening of the face. Ibn 'Atiyya understands "ghabara" as gloom and grief, and "qatara" as the dust of the earth.

Al-Biqa'i and Ibn 'Ashur note that mentioning the blessed before the damned suits the context of the surah, which honours a believer. Al-Razi links the brightness of the faces to freedom from the ties of this world.

This verse describes the faces of the blessed on the Day of Resurrection: they are radiant and bright, laughing and joyful at the honour and favour of God they have received. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most exegetes take the radiance (musfira) to mean brightness, while Ibn Abbas reports that it comes from night prayer, al-Dahhak from ablution, and Ata from the dust suffered in God's cause. Laughter and joy are generally understood as the outward signs of inner delight. Al-Mawardi mentions another possibility: the laughter could be directed at the disbelievers in mockery, but he does not favour it over the first reading. Al-Razi links the radiance to freedom from worldly ties and to union with the sacred realm, and reads laughter and joy as belonging to the theoretical and practical faculties. All agree that these faces belong to the believers, set against the faces covered with dust and darkness of the disbelievers.
