Several commentators connect the verse with the report of Aisha about modesty on the Day of Gathering, presenting it as a response to her concern.

The verse describes the faces of those who disbelieved on the Day of Judgment as covered with dust, ghabara, a dark dust that signifies gloom and sorrow. The commentators offer several explanations. Al-Tabari reports that the dust comes from the beasts which God will turn to dust after judging between them, and that it settles on the faces of the disbelievers. Al-Mawardi gives two readings: a dust placed on them as a mark of shame so they may be recognised, or a metaphor for the darkening of faces by grief. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy describe it as the dejection and sorrow that drain colour from the face of one who is afflicted.

The following word, qatara, is also interpreted in more than one way. Ibn 'Abbas takes it to mean humiliation and distress, Mujahid disgrace, and 'Ata' blackness. Al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd take it to mean dust, with Ibn Zayd distinguishing qatara as what rises towards the sky and ghabara as what settles towards the earth. Al-Kalbi and Muqatil say it is the darkening of the face. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the combination of dust and blackness makes the appearance especially ugly.

The commentators agree that these faces stand in contrast to the radiant faces of the believers described just before, and that their owners are the disbelievers and the wicked. Ibn Kathir explains that disbelief refers to the hearts and wickedness to deeds. Al-Razi reports that the Murji'a and the Khawarij both relied on this passage in their dispute over the grave sinner, and he replies that the verse does not exclude a third category.

This verse describes the faces that will be covered with dust and darkness on the Day of Judgment. These are the faces of disbelievers, who were both unbelieving and wicked in their deeds. Most commentators understand qatara as darkness, blackness and the gloom of the face, as stated by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Muqatil, al-Kalbi, Ibn Kathir, al-Jalalayn and Abu al-Su'ud. Mujahid takes it to mean disgrace, and as-Suddi takes it to mean dust. Ibn Zayd distinguishes qatara, the dust that rises to the sky, from ghabara, the dust that settles on the earth. Al-Mawardi records five closely related views about shame, sorrow and blackness. Al-Razi describes a blackness like smoke, which is especially grim when combined with dust, as is seen on the faces of dark-skinned people covered in dust. Al-Zamakhshari sees in it a reflection of how they joined disbelief with wickedness. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the dust may be a humiliation. The general sense that all of them accept is the contrast with the bright, joyful faces of the believers described just before.

The commentators explain that this verse closes the description of the Day of Resurrection and the division of people into two groups: those whose faces are covered with dust and darkness are the disbelievers and the wicked, meaning those who combined rejection of faith with transgression of God's limits by committing forbidden acts. Most agree that disbelief here refers to rejecting and concealing the truth, and that wickedness refers to departing from obedience to God, neglecting duties and committing prohibitions, as reported by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri. Ibn Kathir takes disbelief to concern the hearts and wickedness the deeds, while al-Nasafi distinguishes the rights of God (disbelief) from the rights of people (wickedness). Al-Mawardi offers two possible readings, either religion and actions, or the rights of God and the rights of people. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shawkani see two inseparable qualities gathered in these people. Al-Razi draws from the verse an argument in the debate between the Murji'a and the Kharijis over the grave sinner, then answers that the text mentions only two groups without excluding a third. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the absence of a conjunction between the two terms indicates that both qualities are found together in them. Al-Alusi and Ibn Sa'di observe that dust and darkness cover them as recompense for denial and wickedness, so that the verse sets the image of misery against the image of happiness that precedes it.
